section.title: The Slaughter of the Idolaters
section.sectionRationale: The vision of idolatry in chapter 8 now meets its answer. Six executioners are summoned, but a seventh man, clothed in linen, goes ahead of them to mark the foreheads of those who grieve over Jerusalem's sins. Only the marked are spared as judgment begins, deliberately, at God's own sanctuary.
section.thesis: God distinguishes with exact care between those who grieve over the abominations filling Jerusalem and those who do not, sparing the marked remnant even as judgment, beginning at His own sanctuary, falls without pity on a city that has filled the land with bloodshed and told itself the LORD does not see.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the six executioners summoned and the man in linen sent to mark the grieving; judgment beginning at the sanctuary itself, sparing only those marked; Ezekiel's anguished plea as he watches the slaughter; and God's answer, that the land's guilt is real and the LORD has not abandoned it without cause.

units.label: The executioners summoned, the man in linen sent to mark
units.note: a mark for those who sigh and groan

verses.text: Then I heard Him call out in a loud voice, saying, “Draw near, O executioners of the city, each with a weapon of destruction in hand.”

And I saw six men coming from the direction of the Upper Gate, which faces north, each with a weapon of slaughter in his hand. With them was another man clothed in linen who had a writing kit at his side. And they came in and stood beside the bronze altar.

Then the {{kavod_2|glory}} of the God of Israel rose from above the cherubim, where it had been, and moved to the threshold of the temple. And He called to the man clothed in linen who had the writing kit at his side.
“Go throughout the city of Jerusalem,” said the LORD, “and put a {{tav|mark}} on the foreheads of the men sighing and groaning over all the abominations committed there.”

units.label: Judgment begins at the sanctuary
units.note: no pity except for the marked

verses.text: And as I listened, He said to the others, “Follow him through the city and start killing; do not show pity or spare anyone!

Slaughter the old men, the young men and maidens, the women and children; but do not go near anyone who has the mark. Now begin at My sanctuary.” So they began with the elders who were before the temple.
Then He told them, “Defile the temple and fill the courts with the slain. Go forth!” So they went out and began killing throughout the city.

units.label: Ezekiel's anguished plea
units.note: will You destroy the entire remnant

verses.text: While they were killing, I was left alone. And I fell facedown and cried out, “Oh, Lord GOD, when You pour out Your wrath on Jerusalem, will You destroy the entire remnant of Israel?”

units.label: The LORD's answer
units.note: the land is full of bloodshed and perversity

verses.text: He replied, “The iniquity of the house of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great. The land is full of bloodshed, and the city is full of perversity. For they say, ‘The LORD has forsaken the land; the LORD does not see.’
But as for Me, I will not look on them with pity, nor will I spare them. I will bring their deeds down upon their own heads.”
Then the man clothed in linen with the writing kit at his side reported back, “I have done as You commanded.”

tav.gloss: A mark, a sign, in the ancient script shaped like a cross or an X. The mark placed on the foreheads of those who grieve over Jerusalem's sin distinguishes them for protection, a pattern echoed in the sealing of God's servants in Revelation 7.

kavod_2.gloss: Glory, the visible presence of God, here seen rising from above the cherubim and moving toward the threshold of the temple, the first step of the departure that will be completed in the following chapters. Even as judgment begins, the glory itself is preparing to leave the corrupted sanctuary.

basic.context: The abominations Ezekiel witnessed in chapter 8 now bring their answer. Six armed executioners are summoned to Jerusalem, but ahead of them goes a seventh figure, a man clothed in linen carrying a scribe's writing kit, sent first to mark the foreheads of everyone who sighs and groans over the city's sins. Only then does the slaughter begin, sparing none but the marked, starting deliberately at the sanctuary itself among the very elders Ezekiel had seen worshiping idols in secret. Ezekiel, watching alone, cries out in anguish, fearing the entire remnant will be wiped out, but God answers that the guilt is real, the land full of bloodshed, and that He will not relent.
basic.hermeneutics: This is a vision of coming judgment carried out in symbolic, dramatic form, deliberately paired with chapter 8's exposure of idolatry, and it should be read as showing God's exact justice, distinguishing the grieving from the complicit, rather than a literal procedural account of how the historical fall of Jerusalem occurred. Its center is the pairing of severe judgment with careful, merciful discrimination for those who mourn evil rather than participate in it.
basic.originalLanguages: The mark placed on the grieving is a tav, a simple mark or sign, in Ezekiel's day likely shaped like a cross, that sets apart those who will be spared. And even as the slaughter begins, the kavod, the glory of God, is seen rising from above the cherubim toward the threshold, the first movement of the departure that chapters 10 and 11 will complete.
basic.typology: The mark on the foreheads of the grieving remnant anticipates the sealing of God's servants on their foreheads in Revelation 7, a pattern of protection amid coming judgment that finds its center in belonging to God through Christ. Judgment beginning at the sanctuary itself anticipates Peter's teaching that judgment begins with the household of God.
basic.christ: The man clothed in linen who marks the grieving before judgment falls anticipates the greater work of Christ, who marks and seals His people with His own Spirit, Ephesians 1:13-14, so that they are distinguished from coming wrath not by their own merit but by belonging to Him. Where judgment here begins at God's own sanctuary among unfaithful elders, Peter later warns that judgment begins with the household of God, 1 Peter 4:17, urging the church toward the very grief over sin that marked those spared in Ezekiel's vision.
basic.god: God is exactingly just, distinguishing precisely between those who grieve over sin and those who commit it without conscience, sparing the mourners even amid sweeping judgment. He is also patient enough to defend His justice to His anguished prophet, showing that even severe judgment is neither careless nor indiscriminate but answers real, extensive guilt.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 12:13 describes another mark that spares from a coming plague, the blood on the doorposts at Passover. Revelation 7:3-4 pictures servants of God sealed on their foreheads before judgment falls. 1 Peter 4:17 teaches that judgment begins with the household of God, echoing this scene's start at the sanctuary.
basic.oneStory: This is the pattern that runs through the whole Bible, judgment falling on real and extensive sin while God marks out and spares a remnant who grieve over evil rather than embrace it, a pattern fulfilled in Christ, who seals His people by His Spirit and shelters them from the wrath that their sin, like Jerusalem's, truly deserves.

context.literary:
Chapter 9 is the middle panel of a single vision that runs from 8:1 to 11:25 and is fenced at both ends by the same sentence: the Spirit lifts Ezekiel up and carries him, to Jerusalem in 8:3 and back to Chaldea in 11:24. Inside that fence the movement is tour, verdict, departure. Chapter 8 walked the prophet past four abominations, each one deeper inside the house than the last: the idol of jealousy at the north gate, seventy elders burning incense to creeping things in a dark room, women weeping for Tammuz, and about twenty-five men with their backs to the temple bowing to the sun, Ezekiel 8:3 to 16. Chapter 9 now turns from what was seen to what must be done about it.

The scene is built around a seventh figure. Six men come with weapons of slaughter, but a man in linen with a scribe's kit comes with them, and he is commissioned first and reports last, 9:2 to 4 and 9:11. The commission to the executioners and the cry of the prophet sit in the middle, so the chapter is framed by the one figure whose task is to save. Notice also the order of the voices. Ezekiel first hears the summons, then sees the men arrive, then hears the instructions, and only after the killing has begun is he allowed to speak, 9:8. For most of the chapter he is a witness with no part.

The chapter also answers chapter 8 line for line. The elders said in 8:12 that the LORD does not see; in 9:9 the LORD quotes them and replies that His eye will not pity. The abominations of chapter 8 were done at the sanctuary, and the sentence begins at the sanctuary, 9:6. The man of 9:11 closes with the only clean report of obedience in the whole four chapters, a short sentence set against a long record of disobedience.
context.historical:
The vision is dated to the sixth year of King Jehoiachin's exile, the sixth month, the fifth day, Ezekiel 8:1, and the first exiles had already been carried to Babylon with their king in 597 BC, 2 Kings 24:14 to 16. Ezekiel himself was among them, a priest by birth, Ezekiel 1:3, sitting with the elders of the exiles at the Kebar. Back in Jerusalem the royal house of Zedekiah governed under Babylonian oversight, and the city was crowded with people who believed that the temple made them untouchable. Jeremiah had been attacking exactly that belief for years, mocking the chant 'This is the temple of the LORD,' Jeremiah 7:4, and warning that God could treat Jerusalem as He had treated Shiloh.

That is the world the vision answers. The people's reasoning is quoted twice, in 8:12 and 9:9: the LORD has forsaken the land, the LORD does not see. It is a strange pair of claims. If He has left, He cannot punish; if He does not see, He cannot know. Either way the way is clear for idols and for the bloodshed that fills the land, 9:9. The vision shows the reverse. He has not left until He chooses to, and He has seen every room.

The historical fulfilment came in 586 BC, when the Babylonians burned the house of the LORD and the whole city, 2 Kings 25:9 and Jeremiah 52:12 and 13. Ezekiel's first hearers in exile were therefore being told, five or six years before the event, that what they would hear about Jerusalem would be a verdict from God and not a failure of His power. That mattered to people who would otherwise conclude that Babylon's gods had beaten the God of Israel. It also served as a warning to exiles who still hoped for a quick return to a safe city.
context.canonical:
The vision draws on the oldest judgment in Israel's memory. In Egypt the destroyer was kept out of every house that bore the blood on its doorframe, Exodus 12:13 and 12:23, and the same Hebrew word for destroyer stands behind the 'weapon of destruction' in Ezekiel 9:1. The pattern is the same, a mark that separates, but the roles are reversed: this time Israel's own house is the Egypt under the sentence, and only a mark of grief protects anyone in it.

The mark returns in Revelation. Before the four angels harm the land, the servants of God are sealed on their foreheads, Revelation 7:2 to 4, and the locusts of the fifth trumpet may harm only those who lack the seal of God on their foreheads, Revelation 9:4. The sealed appear again with the Lamb on Mount Zion, bearing His name and His Father's name, Revelation 14:1, and the last chapter says they will see His face with His name on their foreheads, Revelation 22:4. The beast's counterfeit mark in Revelation 13:16 and 17 imitates the pattern, which shows how much the pattern matters.

The start at the sanctuary is taken up by Peter, who tells suffering believers that it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God, 1 Peter 4:17. Malachi 3:16 to 18 gives a gentler parallel, a scroll of remembrance for those who feared the LORD, when the day comes to distinguish the righteous from the wicked. Jesus' own lament that Jerusalem's house is left desolate, Luke 13:34 and 35, stands in the same line as Ezekiel's vision of the house abandoned.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Ezekiel meant his fellow exiles to hear two things at once and to refuse to choose between them. The first is that the coming fall of Jerusalem is not a mystery and not an accident. It has a cause, which chapter 8 lays out room by room, and it has an author, who stands at the head of the executioners and speaks the sentence. The people of Judah had built a theology that kept God inside the temple like a guarantee, and the vision takes that guarantee apart. A house in which idols are served in the dark is a house under judgment, however many sacrifices are offered at the altar.

The second thing is that judgment is not blind. The man in linen goes first, and his whole task is to find the people who grieve. By telling the exiles about him, Ezekiel opens a door for them. The question the chapter puts to every hearer is which side of the mark they would stand on, whether they share the abominations or sigh over them. Grief over sin, in this chapter, is not a mood. It is the visible sign of belonging to the LORD, set against a city that had stopped being ashamed.

Ezekiel also gives the exiles words for their own prayer. His cry in 9:8 is the cry of someone who loves the people and cannot bear the thought of a total end. The chapter allows that cry and then answers it honestly, without softening the guilt, and the answer opens the hope that grows through chapters 11 and 18 and 36.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes a vision of judgment on one city at one moment; it does not command anyone to kill, and it gives no template for marking out the righteous in any later society. Reading it as a charter for violence against idolaters, or as a method for sorting believers from unbelievers, is a serious mistake. The sword belongs to God and to the agents He appoints in a particular story, and the mark is His to give.

What the chapter does prescribe, by example, is the character of the people it honours. They sigh and groan over the abominations, which is the response of Lot 'tormented in his righteous soul,' 2 Peter 2:8, and of the psalmist whose eyes shed streams of tears because the law is not obeyed, Psalm 119:136. Believers are meant to grieve what dishonours God and not simply to stay clear of it. The chapter also warns that religious position gives no shelter: the first to fall are the elders in front of the temple, and Peter applies the same logic to the church, 1 Peter 4:17. Finally, it permits honest prayer. A prophet who falls on his face and asks whether God will end the remnant is not rebuked for asking.

debates.question: Is the man in linen an angel, a priestly figure, or a pre-incarnate appearance of Christ?

views.label: One of the angelic agents
views.case: He is one of seven men who come together, and he takes his commands from the LORD as the other six do, 9:1 to 4. Linen is the dress of a heavenly figure in Daniel 10:5 and 12:6 and 7. Most commentators take him as an angelic scribe whose office is the opposite of the others, to preserve rather than to destroy.

views.label: A priestly figure
views.case: The linen is the same Hebrew fabric as the sacred tunic of the high priest in Leviticus 16:4. Standing beside the bronze altar, he looks like a priest who has come to make distinctions, and his coals in chapter 10 are taken from the altar fire of the heavenly sanctuary. This reading stresses that the work of marking is a priestly work.

views.label: The Son before He was born
views.case: Some Christian readers see in the man a pre-incarnate Christ because he is the one who acts for the LORD in saving and judging. The text does not identify him, and he takes his orders and reports back to God as a servant would, which fits an angel better.

debates.bearing: The text pictures a commissioned servant who obeys and reports, and that is the safest ground. What he does, though, is what Christ does in the larger story, and the New Testament tells us who actually carries out the sealing of God's people, Ephesians 1:13.

debates.question: Does the judgment really spare the righteous, given Ezekiel 21:3 and 4?

views.label: The mark is a real exemption
views.case: In 9:4 and 9:6 the mark protects. The grieving are alive when the killing ends, and 14:22 promises survivors from Jerusalem who will come to Ezekiel's circle. Ezekiel 18 insists that the righteous will not die for the sins of others, 18:20.

views.label: The mark protects in principle, but the siege still falls on everyone
views.case: Ezekiel 21:3 and 4 says the sword will cut off both the righteous and the wicked, and the siege of 586 BC killed and exiled all kinds of people. On this reading the mark describes God's accounting, which is exact, while the earthly experience of invasion still touches the grieving too, as it touched Jeremiah and Daniel. Isaiah 57:1 notes that the righteous are sometimes taken away from evil rather than spared from it.

views.label: The mark pictures the survival of a remnant, not the safety of each person
views.case: The vision is symbolic and speaks of what God will do with a people, not of every individual. The sealed grieving ones stand for the remnant that comes through to restoration, the people of 6:8 and 11:17 to 20.

debates.bearing: The best reading keeps both texts. God's judgment knows exactly who grieves, and He keeps a people through it, but the Bible never promises believers that nothing in a fallen city's collapse will touch them. The comfort is that the sorting belongs to God and nothing is overlooked.

study.originalLanguages:
Ezekiel 9:1 opens with a word that English has to choose a side on. The BSB has 'executioners of the city.' The Hebrew noun comes from paqad, a root that can mean to visit, to muster, to appoint and to take account, and it is used for visits of blessing and of punishment alike. That is why the same root family gives Isaiah's 'day of reckoning,' Isaiah 10:3. The word here could be read as men appointed over the city, or as the city's reckonings drawing near. Either way, the sense is of an audit coming due.

The weapons carry a deliberate echo. The 'weapon of destruction' in 9:1 uses a form of the verb shachat, to ruin or destroy, and the same root names the destroyer who is kept from the houses of Israel in Exodus 12:23. Ezekiel's first hearers, who knew the Passover story by heart, would have caught the reversal at once: the destroyer is now loosed on Jerusalem.

The linen is bad, the special linen of priests and heavenly figures, Leviticus 16:4 and Daniel 10:5. The mark itself is the tav, and the verb is formed from the same noun, so that the order is almost 'mark a mark.' The mark is placed on the forehead, the most visible place, so the sparing cannot be mistaken. Those who receive it are described by two verbs, sighing and groaning, in the passive or reflexive form that means a continuing, heart-borne grief. The Septuagint renders the tav with the ordinary Greek word for a sign, semeion, which is why the Greek reader hears something close to the seal of Revelation 7. Some early Christian writers, among them Tertullian, saw the shape of a cross in the old form of the Hebrew letter. That is a later reading, not something Ezekiel's text states, and it is better held as a devotional echo than as an argument.

When the sentence is given, it turns on the eye. The LORD says His eye will not spare, which the BSB renders 'I will not look on them with pity,' 9:10, and the whole refrain was already used in 5:11, 7:4 and 8:18. It answers the people's slogan in 9:9, 'the LORD does not see,' with the claim that He sees and will not be moved. The last clause says that He will bring their way, the Hebrew derekh, down on their own heads. The word is the usual one for a person's manner of life, so the judgment is set out as the harvest of what they did, a line Ezekiel repeats in 11:21 and 16:43.

One more word deserves a note. The people say the LORD has forsaken the land, using the verb azav. Moses had warned in Deuteronomy 31:16 and 17 that the people would forsake the LORD and that He would then forsake them. The people read the effect as an excuse and miss the cause.

typology.type: The mark on the forehead, Ezekiel 9:4
typology.fulfillment: A visible sign set on those who belong to God before judgment falls. Revelation 7:3 takes up the pattern when it says the servants of God are sealed on their foreheads, and Revelation 14:1 and 22:4 identify the seal with the name of the Lamb and His Father. Paul uses the cognate idea of an invisible seal: believers are 'sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,' Ephesians 1:13, and told not to grieve Him, Ephesians 4:30. The correspondence runs from a mark of grief to a seal of ownership. It falls short in that Ezekiel's mark was applied to those who were already mourning, while the Spirit's seal is given at faith and then produces the mourning.

typology.type: The destroyer held back by a sign, Exodus 12 and Ezekiel 9
typology.fulfillment: At the first Passover the blood on the doorframe marked a house the destroyer must pass over, Exodus 12:13 and 12:23. Ezekiel's vision recasts the pattern within Israel itself. The mark now is not blood but a condition of heart, and the sentence is carried out against the city that had become Egypt. The New Testament points to the true Passover Lamb, 1 Corinthians 5:7, and to those who are marked as His, Revelation 7:14. The type is incomplete because neither the blood on the doors nor the mark on the foreheads atones for anyone; both point beyond themselves to Christ.

typology.type: Judgment beginning at the sanctuary, Ezekiel 9:6
typology.fulfillment: The sword starts with the elders before the temple, so those with the most light face the earliest reckoning. Peter applies the principle to the church: 'it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God,' 1 Peter 4:17. The same law underlies Jesus' words in Luke 12:48 and the warning of James 3:1 to teachers. The escalation is that, in Christ, the family of God bears the first judgment as discipline, 1 Corinthians 11:32, which leads to cleansing, and not to condemnation. The type breaks down in that the elders of Jerusalem received no such discipline, only the sentence.

typology.type: The man in linen who marks and reports, Ezekiel 9:2 to 11
typology.fulfillment: A figure who moves among the doomed to find and set apart the grieving, and then reports a finished work: 'I have done as You commanded.' Jesus speaks in the same shape when He prays that He has finished the work the Father gave Him, John 17:4, and cries 'It is finished,' John 19:30. He is the High Priest who intercedes for His own, Hebrews 7:25. The correspondence is of function, not identity, since the text does not call the man in linen Christ. The type falls short because the man in linen only distinguishes people, while Christ gives Himself for them.

study.christ:
The chapter does not name Christ, and it should not be forced to. What it gives is a pattern that the New Testament then brings to rest in Him, and the best way to see it is by the three things the vision insists on: a mark, a mediator and a mourner.

The mark is first. Ezekiel's text says that those who grieve are known by a sign on the forehead, and no human hand can fake it. Paul says that believers in Christ have been 'sealed with the promised Holy Spirit,' who is 'the pledge of our inheritance,' Ephesians 1:13 and 14, and that the seal holds 'for the day of redemption,' Ephesians 4:30. The seal of Ezekiel is a hint of a security that does not rest on the believer's grip on God but on God's hold on the believer. Revelation reads the mark as the Lamb's own name, Revelation 14:1 and 22:4, which means the safety of the sealed lies in whose they are.

The mediator comes second. The man in linen walks through a condemned city, and his errand is to protect. He then comes back and says, 'I have done as You commanded.' The Gospel of John gives Jesus nearly the same words, 'I have finished the work You gave Me to do,' John 17:4, and 'It is finished,' John 19:30. The man in linen is not Christ, but in the pattern of obedient service that saves, he stands in the line that leads to Him. Hebrews adds that He lives always to intercede, Hebrews 7:25, which is the thing Ezekiel tried to do in 9:8 and could not finish.

The mourner is third. The Hebrew mark is given to those who grieve, and the one Man who grieved over Jerusalem as no other did was Jesus. He wept over the city and said that its house would be left desolate, Luke 19:41 to 44 and Luke 13:34 and 35, because it had not known the time of its visitation. What Ezekiel saw coming, Jesus saw arriving. Yet He was also the one who bore the sentence in His own body, so that those who belong to Him do not take the sword that the chapter describes. Isaiah 53:11 says the righteous Servant will bear their iniquities.

There is also a reversal worth noticing. In Ezekiel the sentence begins at the sanctuary, among the elders. In the cross, judgment fell on the true Temple, John 2:19 to 21, and fell there for others. Peter can therefore say that judgment begins with the family of God, 1 Peter 4:17, and still call believers to rejoice, because the first and heaviest blow has already been absorbed. Care is needed here: the vision of Ezekiel 9 is about the historical fall of Jerusalem, and its link to Christ runs through the New Testament's own use of the pattern, not through a hidden code.
study.god:
Ezekiel 9 shows a God who is both exact and costly in His justice. The exactness is in the mark. A lesser god would have swept through the city, and a weaker one would have left it alone. The LORD of this chapter tells the executioners to start at the sanctuary and tells the man in linen to go first, and the command is to spare everyone who bears the mark. The accounting is as fine as the verdict is severe. This is the God of Abraham's question, 'Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?', Genesis 18:25, answered in advance.

The chapter also shows a God who sees. The people's whole case rests on the claim that the LORD does not see, 8:12 and 9:9, and the vision is an extended denial. He has watched the elders in the dark room and the men turned toward the sun. He has also watched the sighing in the dark, which is the part that is easy to miss. The same eye that does not pity the guilty marks the grieving. The assertion that 'the LORD does not see' is false in both directions, and it is the grieving who benefit most from the falseness.

He is also a God who does not hide His reasons from a servant. After the killing begins, Ezekiel falls on his face and asks if the whole remnant is to perish. The answer in 9:9 and 9:10 is not a rebuke. It is an explanation: the guilt is very great, the land is full of bloodshed and the city is full of perversity, and He is bringing their conduct on their own heads. God here lets His justice be questioned and answers with evidence. This is the God of Abraham and of Moses, who allows his friends to plead, Exodus 32:11 to 14.

There is a tension that the chapter leaves standing. The LORD is the one who gives the command to defile the temple, 9:7, and the one who will leave it. He is a holy God who is willing to see His own house filled with the dead rather than let it serve as cover for idols. For those who think God is mostly a comfort, this is the necessary correction. For those who think He is mostly a threat, the man in linen is the necessary balance.

For worship, the chapter suggests two postures. The first is reverence before a holiness that does not bend for a building, however sacred. The second is the posture of Ezekiel, facedown, praying even when the answer is hard, and of the nameless group who sigh over what dishonours God. The people God marks are not the ones with the best defence of their city but the ones who share His grief over it.

crossReferences.note: The elders' slogan, 'The LORD does not see us; the LORD has forsaken the land,' is quoted in full here and then again in 9:9. The two chapters are meant to be read as accusation and verdict, and the repetition of the slogan shows exactly which belief the sentence is answering.

The destroyer who is kept out of the houses marked by blood. The Hebrew word for destroyer comes from the same root as the 'weapon of destruction' in Ezekiel 9:1. The mark that once separated Israel from Egypt now has to separate Israelites from Israelites.

An angel with the seal of the living God forbids harm to the land until the servants of God are sealed on their foreheads. This is the clearest New Testament use of the mark of Ezekiel 9:4, and it shows the same logic of a protection that is given before the judgment falls.

Peter writes to believers in suffering and says judgment begins with the family of God. He gives Ezekiel 9:6 a Christian reading: God's house is where His standards are applied first, and the outcome for those outside matters even more.

Jeremiah mocks the chant 'This is the temple of the LORD,' as a deceptive trust. He and Ezekiel preach the same message from two cities, one in Jerusalem and one in exile: God does not protect a building that houses what He hates.

Abraham asks whether the Judge of all the earth will treat the righteous and the wicked alike. Ezekiel's cry in 9:8 is a descendant of that question, and the man in linen is the answer. God does distinguish, and He does so by a means He chooses, not by the city's size or its piety.

The psalmist's eyes shed streams of tears because the law is not obeyed. It is the nearest thing in the Psalms to the sighing and groaning of Ezekiel 9:4, and it shows what a marked person actually looks like: not an outsider, but someone who loves God's law enough to weep when it is broken.

Lot, a righteous man living among the lawless, was 'tormented in his righteous soul' by what he saw and heard day after day. His grief is the pattern for the marked in Jerusalem. God notices the quiet misery of people who cannot stop a city's sin but will not join it.

When the LORD prepares His day, He keeps a scroll of remembrance for those who feared Him, and He says He will spare them as a man spares his own son. The picture is warmer than Ezekiel's but makes the same point: God distinguishes between those who serve Him and those who do not.

Jesus weeps over Jerusalem and foretells its flattening because it did not recognise the time of its visitation. He is describing the Roman siege, not the Babylonian, but He grieves over the same city in the same way, and shows what the marked mourners of Ezekiel's day would have been feeling.

Another cry of the same shape. As Ezekiel prophesies, Pelatiah dies, and the prophet falls on his face to ask whether God will make a complete end of the remnant of Israel. This time the word of the LORD comes with an answer of promise, 11:14 to 21, which is the answer chapter 9 left hanging.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a God who dwells with His people and a world that is very good, Genesis 1:31. The vision of Ezekiel 9 stands at the point where that pattern of dwelling is coming apart for Israel. In Eden, cherubim were stationed at the east to keep humanity from the tree of life, Genesis 3:24, and God's presence was withdrawn from the garden. Here the process repeats at the sanctuary, which was meant to be a small Eden. The people have filled the land with violence, 9:9, as the world had been filled with it before the flood, and the same God who judged then judges now.

But the vision also keeps alive the other thread that runs from Genesis onward. God preserves a remnant. Noah was preserved through the water, and a household was spared at the Passover. A man in linen walks through Jerusalem with a mark. In the book of Ezekiel, the same people appear again as the survivors of 6:8 and 12:16, who will remember the LORD among the nations, and as the people whose heart is changed in 11:19 and 36:26. The mark of chapter 9 is the first stage of a path that leads to a new heart.

The New Testament takes up both threads. The judgment that begins at the household of God, 1 Peter 4:17, is the discipline of a church that lives between the cross and the end. The seal on the foreheads, Revelation 7:3, is the final form of the mark. The one who was sentenced in the place of His people, Isaiah 53:11, has made it possible for people who have shared in the abominations to be counted among those who mourn them.

And the story ends with the undoing of Ezekiel's scene. In the new Jerusalem there is no temple, because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple, Revelation 21:22. There is no one to mark and no need for a man in linen, for the seal is already on every forehead, Revelation 22:4. The grief that marked the faithful in the old city is answered by the promise that God will wipe away every tear and that mourning will be no more, Revelation 21:4. The one who marked the mourners finishes by comforting them.

sermon.title: Corrupt Worship (Part 3)
sermon.why: Carson preaches through Ezekiel 8 and 9 together, showing how the idolatry exposed in chapter 8 leads directly to the marking of the grieving remnant and the judgment carried out by the six executioners in chapter 9.

quiz.q: Who was sent ahead of the six executioners, and for what purpose?

options.text: A seventh executioner with an additional weapon.
options.note: He carries a writing kit, not a weapon, and his task is to mark, not to kill.

options.text: A man clothed in linen, sent to mark the foreheads of those who sigh and groan over Jerusalem's abominations.
options.note: Ezekiel 9:3-4 describes this figure and his protective task.

options.text: A messenger sent to warn the city to flee entirely.
options.note: His task is specifically to mark the grieving for protection, not a general evacuation warning.

options.text: No one was sent ahead of the executioners.
options.note: The man in linen is explicitly sent ahead in verses 3-4.

quiz.q: Where does the slaughter begin, and among whom?

options.text: Outside the city walls first.
options.note: Judgment begins at the sanctuary itself, at the heart of the city, not outside it.

options.text: The passage does not specify where judgment begins.
options.note: Verse 6 specifies the sanctuary and its elders explicitly.

options.text: At God's own sanctuary, beginning with the elders who were before the temple.
options.note: Ezekiel 9:6 states the killing began with the elders at the temple itself.

options.text: In the marketplace among merchants.
options.note: The text specifies the sanctuary and its elders as the starting point.

quiz.q: What did Ezekiel cry out while watching the slaughter?

options.text: He asked God whether He would destroy the entire remnant of Israel.
options.note: Ezekiel 9:8 records this anguished plea.

options.text: He asked to be spared himself.
options.note: His concern in this verse is for the whole remnant of Israel, not merely himself.

options.text: He praised God for swift justice with no concern at all.
options.note: His response is anguished pleading, not untroubled praise.

options.text: He said nothing during the slaughter.
options.note: His cry is recorded directly in verse 8.

quiz.q: How does God answer Ezekiel's anguished question?

options.text: By saying the judgment was a mistake.
options.note: God defends the judgment as just, not mistaken.

options.text: By refusing to answer at all.
options.note: God gives a clear, direct answer in verses 9-10.

options.text: By explaining that the iniquity of Israel and Judah is exceedingly great, full of bloodshed and false claims that the LORD does not see.
options.note: Ezekiel 9:9-10 gives this answer directly.

options.text: By promising to spare everyone regardless of guilt.
options.note: God explicitly says He will not show pity or spare the guilty.

quiz.q: What was happening to the glory of God during this scene?

options.text: It remained fixed and unmoving above the cherubim throughout.
options.note: The text specifically describes movement toward the threshold.

options.text: It had already fully departed from Jerusalem entirely.
options.note: This is only the first movement; full departure comes in later chapters.

options.text: It rose from above the cherubim and moved to the threshold of the temple.
options.note: Ezekiel 9:3 describes this first stage of the glory's departure.

options.text: The glory of God is not mentioned in this chapter.
options.note: Verse 3 explicitly describes the glory's movement.

questions: Those marked for protection were the ones who sighed and groaned over Jerusalem's sin, not merely those who avoided it outwardly. Do you genuinely grieve over sin around you, or do you mostly feel indifferent to it?

Judgment began at God's own sanctuary, among the elders who should have known better. Where might you be tempted to assume that religious position or familiarity with God protects you from taking sin seriously?
Ezekiel pleaded with God on behalf of the remnant even while judgment was underway. Who in your life or community do you need to be pleading for right now, even amid deserved consequences?
God answered Ezekiel's anguish honestly, explaining rather than dismissing his fear. How do you handle it when you bring hard, honest questions to God about suffering or judgment you witness?

Believers are sealed by the Spirit rather than a mark on the skin, yet the pattern is the same: God distinguishes and protects His own before judgment falls. How secure do you feel in Christ's sealing when you consider the reality of final judgment?

translationNotes.note: The mark, tav, was the last letter of the ancient Hebrew alphabet and in its old script resembled a cross or an X shape, a detail often noted though not stated explicitly in the text itself.

The command to begin at My sanctuary is a striking detail: judgment starts not with the pagan nations outside but with God's own people at the very center of worship, underscoring that greater privilege brings greater accountability.
The phrase the LORD does not see directly recalls the elders' words in Ezekiel 8:12, tying this judgment scene explicitly back to the idolatry vision that precedes it.
